## What is longitudinal/repeated measures data

-   Longitudinal data
    -   Measurement of the same subject at different times.
-   Repeated measures data
    -   Measurement of the same subject under different conditions
-   No independence assumption
    -   Varying data analysis approaches
    -   Similar data management approaches
    
::: {.notes}
You will encounter longitudinal data and repeated measures data quite often. Longitudinal data is data where you have multiple measures of the same subject, each measurement at a different time. Repeated measures data is data where you have multiple measures of the same subject, each measurement under a different treatment condition. 

You could argue that repeated measures is just a type of longitudinal data or you could argue that they are quite different. Don't worry too much about this. The thing that both datasets have is the concept of multiple measurements on the same subject. This means that you can't rely on the independence assumption that is required for t-tests, regression, and analysis of variance. The data analytic approaches are quite varied, but the data management for similar for longitudinal data and repeated measures data.
:::

## Longitudinal data

![](../images/babenko-2023.png)

::: {.notes}
Here's an example of longitudinal data from a peer-reviewed artilce. In this study, a residents-as-teachers (RAT) program was evaluated four times: "before and after the RAT program and at one and three years into practice". The researchers measured "interest, comfort, confidence, skill, familiarity with aspects of clinical teaching".  
:::

## Repeated measures data

![](../images/smits-2016.png)

::: {.notes}
Here is an example of repeated measures data in a peer-reviewed article. Sixteen subjects born in the Netherlands, but fluent in English, were given both the Dutch and the American English versions of the digits-in-noise test. This is a test used to diagnose hearing loss. Both versions were presented with different background noises. They were also tested in the left ear along, the right ear alone, both ears, and a dichotic condition (different sounds placed in the left and right ear). Each subject had to listen to the two language version times two noise conditions times four ear conditions. This represents 16 measures on each person.
:::


## Time-constant and Time-varying data

-   Time constant data
    -   Does not change across time/repeated measures
    -   Should be stored as one row per patient
-   Time varying data
    -   Changes across time/repeated measures
    -   Could be stored one row per patient
    -   Could be stored one row per time/measure

::: {.notes}
When you have longitudinal data or repeated measures, it helps to classify every variable as either time-constant or time-varying.

Time-constant data is data that is fixed across all time points or across all repeated measures. Most demographic variables are time-constant. A patients gender or race is generally the same. If you have age, you might consider age at the start of the study as a time-constant variable.

Time constant data is best stored as one row per patient rather than one row per time point or measurement.

Time varying data changes from one time point to another or from one repeated measurement condition to another. Your outcome variables in either setting would be considered time-varying data. Some covariates that change over time or with different measurement conditions would be time-varying data. In a study of developmental milestones during puberty, age at the time of each visit would be time-varying data.

Time varying data could be stored as one row per subject with the varying values represented as a sequence of columns. This is known as the wide format. 

It could also be stored as one row per time point with the varying values represented as a sequence of rows. This is known as the tall format.

There are some gray areas besides age where it is unsure whether a variable is time-constant or time-varying. Don't worry too much about this. The context in which you collected your data should allow you to make the appropriate distinction.
:::

## The wide format

$\begin{matrix}
1 & O_{11} & O_{12} & O_{13} & O_{14} & A_1 & B_1 & \cdots \\
2 & O_{21} & O_{22} & O_{23} & O_{24} & A_2 & B_2 & \cdots \\
3 & O_{31} & O_{32} & O_{33} & O_{34} & A_3 & B_3 & \cdots \\
4 & O_{41} & O_{42} & O_{43} & O_{44} & A_4 & B_4 & \cdots \\
4 & O_{51} & O_{52} & O_{53} & O_{54} & A_5 & B_5 & \cdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & 
\end{matrix}$


::: {.notes}
How would the outcome measured at the four time points in the longitudinal study be stored? There are two formats, the wide format and the long format. Here is the data stored in the wide format.

The first column (1, 2, 3, 4, ...) is an identification number that indicates which subject is which. It doesn't have to be a strict sequence like shown here. It could be a medical record number, for example, but you do want to be careful with medical record numbers from a confidentiality perspective.

The next four columns represent the outcome, arranged horizontally. The double subscript used here is interpreted as follows. The first subscript identifies which subject and the second subscript identifies the time point in the longitudinal study.

The remaining columns represent additional variables that are not repeated. The columns might represent demographics about the subject such as age and gender. Since these are not time-varying, you only need a single subscript.

Strictly speaking, you do not need an identification number when the data is in the wide format, but it is a good practice to follow.
:::

## The long format

$\begin{matrix}
1 & 1 & O_{11} & A_1 & B_1 & \cdots \\
1 & 2 & O_{12} & A_1 & B_1 & \cdots \\
1 & 3 & O_{13} & A_1 & B_1 & \cdots \\
1 & 4 & O_{14} & A_1 & B_1 & \cdots \\
2 & 1 & O_{21} & A_2 & B_2 & \cdots \\
2 & 2 & O_{22} & A_2 & B_2 & \cdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots& \vdots & \vdots &
\end{matrix}$

::: {.notes}
Here is what the data looks like in the long format. The first column is the identification number. You definitely need this. You also need a column that tells you whether this is the first, second, third, or fourth longitudinal measure. The outcome is arranged vertically in a single column. The remaining columns represent additional variables. Since these are not time-varying, you need to repeat these values four times.  
:::

## Which format is better?

-   Neither is uniformly superior
-   Long format
    -   Time constant data is repeated
    -   Extra space requirements
    -   Increase chance for data quality problems
-   Wide format
    -   Excessive number of columns
    -   Difficult to scroll left/right
-   Different analyses require different formats
    -   Correlations need the wide format
    -   Plots require the long format

::: {.notes}
You might ask which approach is superior. It turns out that neither approach is uniformly superior. The long format has multiple rows for each patient which requires repetition of the time-constant data. This creates extra space requirements for the dataset. This is not an issue for small and moderate size datasets, but can be a problem for very large datasets.

More importantly, the repetition increases the chances for data quality problems. A small typographical error could convert a male patient into a female patient halfway through a longitudinal study or reclassify a pediatric patient as a senior citizen.

The wide format can has an excessive number of columns. This depends on the number of time points or repeated measures, but it often makes a dataset unwieldy.

Scrolling left and right on a computer screen is more difficult than scrolling up and down. Your computer has a Page Up and a Page Down key, but it does not have Page Left and Page Right keys. Even if it did, it is very easy visually to accidentally jump up or down a line of data when there are lots of columns to scroll through.

Have you noticed how newspapers will print their articles. No article spans the entire page, which in a newspaper is quite wide. Instead, the articles are placed in relatively narrow columns. The reason for this is if you are reading a very wide line of text, when you reach the end of a line and have to jump back to the beginning, it is difficult to start a fresh line. It takes a very disciplined eye to trace back to the left side of the page and do so without straying up or down. It's best to keep the articles to about 40 characters of text. The eye doesn't have to work as hard and you can more easily jump to the start of the correct line.

A bigger problem is missing values. If a subject drops out after the second of ten longitudinal measurements, that subject just has two lines in the long format. But you have to keep the ten columns of longitudinal measurements for that subject because other subjects will need all of those columns. The result is missing values for 8 of the 10 columns. As a general rule, you want to try to minimize the use of missing value codes because they create such problems. 

It turns out that different analyses require different formats. Correlations, for example, require the wide format while most plots require the long format.
:::
